stem.text: Let \( f(x) = 2 x^{3} \sin{\left(\frac{1}{x} \right)} - 1 \) for \( x \ne 0 \). Find \( \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) \), and justify your answer.

answer_key.label: The limit is -1, because \( -1 - 2 \left|{x}\right|^{3} \le f(x) \le 2 \left|{x}\right|^{3} - 1 \) for \( x \ne 0 \) and both bounds approach -1 as x approaches 0.

worked_solution.text: Multiplying by the nonnegative quantity \( 2 \left|{x}\right|^{3} \) and adding -1 gives \( -1 - 2 \left|{x}\right|^{3} \le f(x) \le 2 \left|{x}\right|^{3} - 1 \). The factor \( 2 x^{3} \) can be negative, so its absolute value is used to keep the inequality true.
Both bounds are continuous, so their limits as x approaches 0 are both -1.

options.label: The limit is -1, because \( - 2 x^{3} - 1 \le f(x) \le 2 x^{3} - 1 \) for \( x \ne 0 \) and both bounds approach -1 as x approaches 0.
options.derivation: the bounds of the oscillating factor multiplied by the sign changing factor without reversing the inequality where it is negative
